objectives: 1. State how Paul's training and experience in Judaism helped prepare

blocks.x: The more you know about an author, the better you understand his
writings. Before you start to study Galatians, let's look at the person who
wrote this epistle—the great apostle Paul. The more you know about his
personal characteristics and experiences, the more clearly you will see
why he wrote what he did. Throughout Galatians, we will see Paul
defending the Christian faith against the Judaizers. You have already read
about the importance of this epistle. Now let's see how God prepared Paul
through education and experience to write it.

blocks.x: A. Defense of the Faith Needed in Galatia
Objective 1: Show the importance of Paul's letter to the Galatians in
meeting the crisis of legalism.
When we mention the crisis in Galatia, three questions come to our minds:
1) Who were the Galatians? 2) What was the crisis? 3) What was Paul's
responsibility? Answering these questions will help you to see more
easily the purpose and structure of the book of Galatians.
1. The Galatians
Objective 2: Use a map to explain who the Galatians were.
Read Galatians 1:1-2. To whom does Paul address this letter?
Read these passages in Acts and name the cities where the
people received the message gladly but later turned against Paul.
14 • Galatians
Look at the map of Paul's Missionary Journeys (pp. vii-viii). Find
Antioch (in Galatia), Lystra, Iconium, and Derbe.
On which missionary journeys did Paul visit Antioch, Lystra,
Iconium, and Derbe?
Paul founded several churches in the southern part of the Roman
administrative province of Galatia. Sometimes the province was called
Lycaonia. We believe that he wrote this epistle to the churches in this area.
Objective 3: Use a chronology chart to explain when this epistle was
written.
Match the events of Paul’s life to the dates.
Paul’s travel to Jerusalem for the Council • • 49 AD
Paul’s execution in Rome • • 45-49 AD
Paul’s first missionary journey • • 49 or 50 AD
The writing of Paul’s letter to Galatians • • 68 AD
The southern area was already evangelized at the close of the first
missionary journey. It seems that Paul wrote this letter shortly after his
first missionary journey and just before his journey to the Jerusalem
Council in A.D. 49. We know that the subjects Paul wrote about in
Galatians were dealt with in the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). If this had
taken place already, Paul would surely have mentioned the decisions of
the council in Galatians. The council definitely decided that Gentile
Christians would not have to be circumcised or keep the Jewish laws.
Since Paul does not mention this ruling, we may suppose that Galatians
was written before the Jerusalem Council.

blocks.x: A. Gospel of Faith Received by Galatians (3:1-5)
Objective 1: Appreciate Paul's firm stand on the Scriptures and the
importance of this principle in your own ministry.
In the previous lessons Paul's argument has been based on his personal
experience in the gospel. Now he turns to the Scriptures and shows that
his spiritual experience is grounded on the word of God.
Whom does Paul blame for the doctrinal error in the Galatian
churches? v. 1
a) Demonic forces
b) The Judaizers
c) The Galatians themselves
d) The church in Jerusalem
Why does Paul blame the Galatians?
State in your own words what Paul is saying in Galatians 3:3.
Paul emphasizes here that the Christian life is supernatural from
beginning to end. In verse 4 he asks the Galatians, “Did you have such
wonderful spiritual experiences all for no purpose?”
On what basis does God bless the ministry of some people today,
saving many souls, pouring out his Spirit, healing the sick, or
causing their churches to grow? 3:5
58 • Galatians
B. Gospel of Faith Given to Abraham (3:6-9)
Objective 2: Describe the role of Abraham in the history of redemption
and your relationship to him.
Objective 3: Explain what it means to be justified by faith.
Paul now shows the Galatians that the gospel of faith they received is the
same one that was given to Abraham many centuries before. Their
experience was rooted in the word of God and also in the history of God's
people. In his theological argument Paul shows that God's method of
justifying men has always been by faith. To prove it, Paul uses Abraham
as an example and quotes the good news given to him.
Why is Abraham an appropriate example?
a) Because he knew Jesus personally.
b) Because he was a Gentile like the Galatians.
c) Because he was under the law.
d) Because he had no children at that moment.
According to Galatians 3:6 how was Abraham made right with
God? What was it that was put to his account as righteousness?
Read Genesis 15:1-6 to acquaint you with the context of the
verse that Paul quotes. Copy the verse in Genesis that Paul
quotes.
According to verse 7 who are the true descendants of Abraham?
How does verse 8 say that God was going to justify the Gentiles?
Who shall be blessed in Abraham? 3:8

blocks.x: A. From Bondage to Sonship (4:1-5)
Objective 1: Distinguish between being a slave and a son spiritually
and apply this truth in your life and ministry.
1. Bondage of Infancy (4:1-3)
The idea of the law as a guardian which you saw in Galatians 3:24
continues in Chapter 4. You remember that the paidagogos was the
teacher or escort for very small children. Here we find Paul speaking of a
child under guardians and managers (tutors and governors) until the child
is of age. See verse 2. These guardians represent the law. Here the Jew is
pictured as the young child.
What does Paul say that this child is? 4:1
What was the child’s condition like? 4:1
70 • Galatians
What do the guardians represent?
a) The law
b) The Son
c) The Father
Verse 1 compares the child heir with slaves. If the child is the Jew, we
might say that the slaves are the Gentiles in this picture.
Compare the rights and opportunities of the child and of the
slaves in verse 1.
Paul is saying here that these two groups of humanity—Jew and
Gentile—were both under bondage. Both were on the same level.
How does verse 3 describe this period of childhood under the
control of guardians?
“The elementary principles of the world” is also translated as “the
elemental things of the world.” This refers to basic instruction—such as
teaching the alphabet. These words can include the elementary principles
of the world system, ceremonial religions of both Jews and Gentiles.
